overview.title: Bag-of-words encoding of IMDb with TextVectorization
overview.main_topic: Using Keras's TextVectorization layer with adapt() and multi-hot output to turn IMDb reviews into 20,000-dimensional bag-of-words vectors
overview.central_idea: Instead of extending the hand-written WordTokenizer, you can use Keras's TextVectorization layer. It splits on whitespace, learns a 20,000-word vocabulary with adapt() on the label-free training texts, and outputs multi-hot vectors. Mapping it over all three Datasets gives batches of shape (32, 20000), ready for a linear model.
overview.importance: This is the practical implementation of the bag-of-words idea from p.422. The same layer and the same adapt() pattern are reused for bigrams (p.427), padded integer sequences (p.430) and the character-level tokenizer in chapter 15 (p.448).

Configure TextVectorization for word-level multi-hot output
Explain what adapt() does and why it is called on a label-free Dataset
Apply a preprocessing layer inside a tf.data pipeline with map and num_parallel_calls
Predict the batch shapes produced by the pipeline

summary:
The page first completes the toy example from p.422. In `[1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]`, the 0 in the **fifth position** means `"laugh"` is absent, and the 1 in the **sixth position** means `"cry"` is present (positions counted from 1). This simple encoding can be used directly to train a model.

**Section 14.4.1, Training a bag-of-words model.** You could extend the `WordTokenizer` written earlier in the chapter, but it is easier to use Keras's built-in **`TextVectorization`** layer. It handles word and character tokenization and has extra features, including **multi-hot encoding** of its output.

Like many Keras preprocessing layers, `TextVectorization` has an **`adapt()`** method that learns layer state from data. Here that state is a **vocabulary**, built on the fly by iterating over a dataset. The authors choose **20,000 words**, which they call a good starting place for text classification.

**Listing 14.12**:

- creates `TextVectorization(max_tokens=20_000, split="whitespace", output_mode="multi_hot")` (callout: 'Learns a word-level vocabulary');
- strips labels with `train_ds.map(lambda x, y: x)` and calls `adapt` on the resulting text-only Dataset;
- maps `lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y)` over the train, validation and test Datasets with `num_parallel_calls=8`, producing `bag_of_words_train_ds`, `bag_of_words_val_ds` and `bag_of_words_test_ds`.

A quick inspection of one batch, `next(bag_of_words_train_ds.as_numpy_iterator())`, shows `x.shape == (32, 20000)`: 32 reviews, each a 20,000-dimensional presence/absence vector. The printed `y.shape` is `(32, 1)`. (Note: with the default integer labels of Listing 14.11 you may see `(32,)` instead; see the review flag.) The next page builds a linear model with 20,001 parameters on these inputs (p.424).

paragraphs.excerpt: The TextVectorization layer, like many preprocessing layers in Keras, has an adapt()
paragraphs.what_it_says: TextVectorization, like many Keras preprocessing layers, has an adapt() method that learns layer state from data. For TextVectorization, adapt() learns a vocabulary by iterating over an input dataset. The authors use it to tokenize and encode the data with a 20,000-word vocabulary, a good starting place for text classification.
paragraphs.what_it_means: adapt() is not gradient training. It is a single pass that counts token frequencies and keeps the most frequent max_tokens entries (including the reserved [UNK]). After that, the mapping is fixed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The vocabulary size sets the input dimension of the model (20,000) and therefore its parameter count (20,001 on p.424). Learning it only from training data avoids leaking validation or test information.
paragraphs.technical_idea: This is the same pattern as Normalization.adapt() learning a mean and variance: preprocessing layers carry state that is computed from data, not learned by backpropagation.

concepts.name: TextVectorization layer
concepts.definition: A Keras preprocessing layer that standardizes, splits and indexes text and can output integer sequences or encodings such as multi-hot.
concepts.intuition: A configurable 'text-to-numbers' machine whose dictionary you fill by showing it your training data.
concepts.technical: Key arguments on this page: max_tokens=20_000, split="whitespace", output_mode="multi_hot". The output for a batch of N strings has shape (N, max_tokens).
concepts.significance: It replaces the hand-written tokenizers for all of chapter 14's experiments.
concepts.example: text_vectorization(["great movie"]) gives a 1×20000 vector with ones at the IDs of 'great' and 'movie'.
concepts.misconception: That split="whitespace" means no standardization. Lowercasing and punctuation stripping still apply by default (beyond the book).

concepts.name: adapt() for preprocessing layers
concepts.definition: Computing a preprocessing layer's internal state from a dataset before training.
concepts.intuition: Building the dictionary before you start translating.
concepts.technical: TextVectorization.adapt iterates over a Dataset of strings, counts tokens and keeps the top max_tokens. It must receive text only, which is why the labels are stripped with map(lambda x, y: x).
concepts.misconception: That adapt() updates weights by gradient descent. It is a statistics pass.

concepts.name: Multi-hot encoding
concepts.definition: A vocabulary-length binary vector marking which tokens are present.
concepts.technical: output_mode="multi_hot" gives a float vector of length 20,000 per review.
concepts.significance: It is the input representation of the bag-of-words model.
concepts.example: Toy: [1,1,0,1,0,1]; position 5 ('laugh') is 0 and position 6 ('cry') is 1.
concepts.misconception: That position numbers in the text are 0-based. 'Fifth position' means index 4.

concepts.name: Preprocessing inside tf.data with map
concepts.definition: Applying a function, here the vectorization layer, to every element of a Dataset, optionally in parallel.
concepts.intuition: An assembly line that turns raw reviews into vectors while the model is training.
concepts.technical: ds.map(lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8) transforms only the inputs and keeps the labels. Eight elements are processed concurrently.
concepts.significance: It keeps preprocessing on the CPU, in parallel with model computation.
concepts.misconception: That map runs once and stores results. It is lazy and runs each time the Dataset is iterated, unless .cache() is used (beyond the book).

code.title: Applying a bag-of-words encoding to the IMDb reviews
code.original_code:
from keras import layers

max_tokens = 20_000
text_vectorization = layers.TextVectorization(
    max_tokens=max_tokens,
    split="whitespace",
    output_mode="multi_hot",
)
train_ds_no_labels = train_ds.map(lambda x, y: x)
text_vectorization.adapt(train_ds_no_labels)

bag_of_words_train_ds = train_ds.map(
    lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8
)
bag_of_words_val_ds = val_ds.map(
    lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8
)
bag_of_words_test_ds = test_ds.map(
    lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8
)
code.what_it_does: Builds a word-level TextVectorization layer with multi-hot output, learns a 20,000-token vocabulary from the training texts, and converts all three Datasets into (multi-hot vector, label) batches.

Learns the vocabulary from the 20,000 training reviews only, never from validation or test data.
Applies the layer to the inputs of every batch in train, val and test, keeping the labels. num_parallel_calls=8 runs up to 8 map calls concurrently.

deeper.title: Why fit the vocabulary only on training data?
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the vocabulary is a statistic of the data, the top 20,000 most frequent tokens. If you computed it on validation or test reviews, word choices from held-out data would shape the features, which is a mild form of information leakage. Listing 14.12 adapts on `train_ds_no_labels` only and then applies the frozen mapping everywhere. Words that appear only in test reviews simply map to `[UNK]`.

deeper.title: What 20,000 tokens covers
deeper.body: Beyond the book: word frequencies follow a roughly Zipfian distribution, so a few thousand words cover most running text. IMDb has on the order of 100k distinct whitespace tokens, but capping at 20,000 keeps nearly all frequent sentiment words while discarding rare names and typos into `[UNK]`. This is a reasonable trade-off for a linear model with 20,001 parameters (p.424).

questions.question: Why does Listing 14.12 call train_ds.map(lambda x, y: x) before adapt()?
options: Because adapt() needs only the text, not the labels
To speed up training of the model
questions.answer: Because adapt() needs only the text, not the labels
questions.explanation: adapt() builds the vocabulary from strings, so the labels must be stripped. The map does not shuffle, does not split data, and is not related to model training speed.

questions.question: What are the shapes of x for one batch from bag_of_words_train_ds, and what does each dimension mean?
questions.answer: (32, 20000): 32 reviews per batch × 20,000 vocabulary slots (presence flags).
questions.explanation: batch_size=32 comes from Listing 14.11 and max_tokens=20,000 from Listing 14.12.

questions.question: Why should adapt() be run on the training set only, and not on validation or test data?
questions.answer: The vocabulary is derived from data. Fitting it on held-out data would let information from those sets influence preprocessing (leakage), and the validation and test sets should simulate unseen data.
questions.explanation: The listing adapts on train_ds_no_labels only and reuses the fitted layer for val and test.

questions.question: Which TextVectorization argument makes the output a presence vector rather than a sequence of token IDs?
questions.explanation: output_mode controls the encoding. split chooses word-level tokenization, max_tokens caps the vocabulary, and num_parallel_calls is an argument of Dataset.map, not of the layer.

questions.question: A linear model on these inputs has one weight per vocabulary entry plus a bias. How many parameters is that, and how many float32 values does one input batch contain?
questions.explanation: p.424 confirms the 20,001 parameters. The batch size follows from the printed x.shape.

questions.question: In [1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1], which word does the 'fifth position' refer to, and is it present?
questions.explanation: The book counts positions from 1, so the fifth position is index 4 of the vocabulary {[UNK]:0, movie:1, film:2, made:3, laugh:4, cry:5}.

questions.question: Could you swap split="whitespace" for split="character" and predict what the multi-hot vectors would look like? Would that be a good idea for sentiment?
questions.answer: Each vector would mark which characters appear, and almost every review contains nearly every letter, so the vectors would be nearly identical. That is a poor idea, as p.426 notes.
questions.explanation: p.426 explains that a bag of characters tells you very little about a review's content.
